doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Music is feeling, not technique
summary: Nussbaum says great art projects a feeling, naming Ben Webster, Coltrane, Hendrix and Holiday.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: And it can’t be — what you’re talking about can’t be because of your technique I wouldn’t think.
You’re talking to the wrong people here about that.
I mean it’s something else, right? It’s making connections between players, and I mean I don’t know what. But maybe we can’t describe it but you’re feeling it in the last year or so you said.

I just feel like I’m getting a better idea about music and projecting that other thing which can’t really be described or explained. You know it’s not a technical thing. It’s not necessarily an intellectual thing. It’s more a vibe that’s being created and maybe you want to call it a spiritual kind of feeling. But projecting a feeling and having people being able to feel something through the music. I mean I realize that recently this is a gift if you can play music and get out there and play for people. You have a certain amount of gift. That maybe you just God dropped it in your lap or maybe you’ve spent a lot time working at the craft to have this gift. And then when you get out you’re trying to make people feel something hopefully. Any great artist is going to do that to you in any field of music and any kind of art idiom. Picasso could do it, Rembrandt could do it, Ben Webster could do it with one note, John Coltrane could do it with a thousand notes. You know what I’m saying? And Jimi Hendrix could do it. Marvin Gaye could do it. You get a vibe. You get a feeling. Billie Holiday.
You name it. Humphrey Bogart. Greta Garbo.
Yeah. That’s, you know that’s so true. Like Humphrey did it with like his look or a look.
Someone else did it with a note.
